item.content:encoded: FirstDateback in AprilHow will the matchmaking work? What questions are even in the matchmaking questionnaire? (Read on for the full list)On FirstDate’s website, one line stands out: “FirstDate uses a Nobel prize-winning framework called the Gale-Shapley Stable Marriage Algorithm”. It’s a brow-raising detail because, despite the name, the algorithm has almost nothing to do with marriage, but more on this later.The dating service will use Singpass to verify the identity of users, match people in cycles (you get only one match each cycle), and share contact details only when both users agree to their match.To get a sense of how the matchmaking works, here’s the questionnaire that the government workers signing up must fill out. The questions are a mix of close-ended and open-ended ones, across 8 categories, spanning topics like interests and passions, lifestyle and daily habits, and communication and relationship style.What are you into these days?Now, spill! What do you actually love about your hobbies? What cuisines do you eat on repeat and never get sick of?Which restaurant do you keep going back to and why?How often do you find an excuse to leave the country?What kind of traveler are you, really? What’s a country that’s ruined all other countries for you? Team sunrise, or team “it’s 2am and I’m still up”?Gym rat, occasional jogger, or exercise is a myth to you? Any food rules we should know about? Be honest! What does your room look like right now?Hustle mode, or protecting your personal time?Real talk. How much of your day disappears into your phone?Describe your social energy. Are you the life of the party, or the one who left an hour ago? How important is it for you that a match brings the same energy, or do opposites attract for you? After a brutal work week, what’s your reset button? New city, new hobby, new anything. How do you feel about the unknown?When you’re feeling a lot, what do you actually do about it?How do you like to be loved? Non-stop texting, or comfortable silence. Where do you land?Mid-disagreement, what’s your gut instinct? Paint us a picture. What does your dream first date look like? What are your non-negotiable green flags in a partner? Are you always working on yourself, or is “good enough” good enough? Do you see yourself having children? Saver, spender, or “I’ll figure it out eventually”?What’s your religion, if any? Any hard nos for you? Be honest, we won’t judge.What’s the youngest age you’d consider dating? What’s the oldest age you’d consider dating?Write a short note for your future match! Tell us about yourself in a few sentences. After a question about the name you prefer to go by and your mobile number, the questionnaire also collects information about how many first dates you’ve been on in the past year, whether you’ve used a dating app or matchmaking service before, and when you last went on a first date.But how will the rest of the data collected through these questions be used? The fascinating history of the Gale-Shapley Stable Marriage Algorithm (also known as the deferred acceptance algorithm) gives us some clues.Before the algorithm earned its name, a similar system was used to match medical school residents with residency programmes in hospitals in the United States since the 1950s. After an interview process, doctors and hospitals provide a rank ordered list of their preferences, which the algorithm turns into a stable match.What makes the match stable is that after all the matching has concluded, no pair would rather be paired with one another over their current partners.Confused? This YouTube video explains it better than I can:What made the algorithm so novel was that it proved that such a stable match always exists when there are equal participants of each type (and that there is a solution to achieve it). The 2012 Nobel Prize in economics went to one of the mathematicians who developed the algorithm (Shapley) and an economist who pointed out the medical resident example and used it to develop other real world applications.It’s called a marriage algorithm because the theory used marriage proposals as a memorable but theoretical example. The real world applications of the algorithm (like school choice systems) tend to have little to do with dating, for reasons that I’ll elaborate on below.What does this mean for those signing up to FirstDate? Well, the algorithm is why FirstDate’s matching takes place in what its developers call “cycles” or “programmatic rounds”.Presumably, the algorithm uses each user’s questionnaire answers to rank all participants of the opposite gender based on compatibility. The algorithm then matches everyone until all couples are in stable matches (see above).After you decide to say yes or no to your match, that’s it for the cycle. You’ll have to wait for the next one to get a new stable match with a new pool of participants.From my perspective, there are three glaring issues that emerge when applying this kind of game theory to dating:(Side note: While the nature of the algorithm might imply that same-sex pairings are not possible, other dating-related implementations of the algorithm have allowed for same-sex pairings. It is doubtful that this will happen here though, because, well, Singapore.)All of this is further complicated when there are outside options. Like, say, other online dating services or your workplace crush who isn’t participating in the process. Because there is no commitment to the process (because this isn’t your state-assigned waifu, thank god), the maths that underpins the algorithm doesn’t really make sense.claimsIn short, stable matches mean nothing when nobody is committed and the best options might exist outside of the matchmaking pool.interviewedAphrodite ProjectIf you’re a gym rat, does that mean you also want to match with other gym rats? The problem with modern dating is a problem of mismatched preferences!According to FirstDate’s website, it “started with a question among a group of GovTech officers: does having more potential matches necessarily make it easier to find a suitable match?”This is a similar diagnosis to what the folks behind the Aphrodite Project came to, but I feel that it captures an incomplete part of the whole picture.The rise of online dating paralleled the rise of a particular way of thinking about love that’s more checklist oriented than it is holistic, where daters increasingly screen their options ahead of time against a predetermined list of green and red flags.How does a system for matchmaking people account for the fact that the people who need matchmaking also tend to be the worst at understanding what they really want in a relationship?Let me paint you a picture of what seems to be the common dating experience in Singapore: You’re on a first date with someone in a chain restaurant in a mall somewhere in central Singapore. The conversation revolves almost entirely around the biodata and information that HR and recruiters would collect from you.Where do you live? Where did you study? What job do you have?There’s nothing innately wrong with having preferences relating to these things, but dating that’s all about these preferences betrays a deeply transactional and instrumentalist view of love that sees other people not as potential life partners, but pathways to potential lifestyles. Not lovers, but co-owners of a financial venture. Not people, but breeders of sought-after children.It’s a mindset that’s enabled by the market-driven logic of dating apps, where we commodify ourselves to score swipes. It’s also a mindset that gives intensely unattractive only child energy.In Singapore, this transactional view is only sharpened and reinforced by policies like the BTO system for public housing, where the rational move for financially savvy couples is to apply before marriage, often while one is still studying, so that they can get the best subsidies.For these couples, it means that they’ll likely have spent no time at all living with their partner-to-be, and navigating messy questions of how you actually are in states of boredom and stress. Instead, they’re spending all their time planning for their financial futures and screening their partner in terms of their viability for a rigid life path.increase the fertility rateIt is also telling that before the launch of FirstDate, its developers sent out a survey to prospective users on CrowdTask (the government’s survey platform) asking them why they want to be in a relationship.Perhaps that’s filed under “other” or “enjoying romantic intimacy”?tend to have similar valueslove languageWhat I am saying is that perhaps, we shouldn’t be treating our choice of partners with the same mindset as how we approach schools and jobs, through the lens of competition in pursuit of optimal choices. Or through an algorithm used for matching people to their schools and workplaces.To be clear, I do think that this GovTech pilot programme is an admirable initiative. More experimentation in the public sector is always a net positive, and I hope this doesn’t read as me just clowning on a good faith attempt at fixing what’s wrong with online dating.There are clear benefits to a model of online dating driven less by profit incentives and shareholder value, and driven more by user needs.‘Single, Desperate and Ugly’points outStill, if the goal of FirstDate is to make a better product than dating apps, they’ve already succeeded (for hetero sinkies aged 21 to 35). But, mind you, the bar is in hell.enshittificationI’m not convinced that a better algorithm is the solution (though I’d be glad to be proven wrong). Really, the clamouring for it is symptomatic of our redpilled and incel-inflected times.The truth is that we don’t really know what exactly makes love work, such that we can articulate and implement it on a societal scale. It’s too messy, too complex, too idiosyncratic, and too human. Anyone who claims otherwise probably has a course to sell you on negging and pickup artistry.I bought the meals, spent so much time offering my shoulder to them, gave so much of myself to them, and they still chose someone else. they’re all just gold diggers, people only value appearance, nice guys finish last.(I want to scream: love is not a rank ordered list!!)interviewing incels and former incelsRather than creating an off-ramp from a system of alienating self-commodification, FirstDate creates another platform for people to game.There’s a good reason why Singaporeans are still – according to surveys by the National Population and Talent Division at least – more likely to find love through offline methods (their schools, workplaces, family friends) than online channels.decliningThe urge to quantify compatibility is understandable. This is Singapore after all, a country where we just can’t resist tying our self worth to a score. But, even a casual look around you at the couples that do work would tell you that this impulse to quantify defies logic.If the man I’m marrying in January were to fill out this questionnaire, he’d probably fill it out like an introspective soft boy and express a preference for softspoken people that fit into that lifestyle.(as a queer person, this is strictly a hypothetical)The result would likely mean being matched up to somebody like our exes.Instead, we met over Grindr, an app where one has little to go off of besides appearance, distance, and sexual compatibility. And over the next year, he became my plus one to all the nightclubs and bars and parties I write about as a lifestyle journalist. And he, in turn, drags me out to the fandom conventions and game jams that he loves (and that I admittedly am lukewarm on). I fell in love with him on the dancefloor, and he fell in love with me during the quiet times in between.I’d argue this surprise and unpredictability is key to finding chemistry.spend so much time in the rat raceSo, here’s my proposal: Let’s fund culture clubs, theatre groups, video game conventions, music festivals, whatever!Instead of promoting them as places where people can come to meet their prospective partners (you’ll be accused of trying to resurrect the Single, Desperate, and Ugly club), let’s bet that happy and fulfilled people with friends and access to thriving third spaces will couple up if they want to.Instead of ramming pro-fertility rhetoric down our throats, let’s focus instead on eroding the barriers that so many people feel when it comes to being part of a community, like the steep cost of just existing in public in capitalist Singapore or the exorbitant cost of late night transportation or the reality that it’s hard to have friends over (let alone a prospective date) when one is expected to live with their family until their 30s.Let’s focus on broadening the extremely narrow horizon of social possibility in Singapore, where everyone complains that there is no nature, no culture, and nothing to do but eat and sleep and travel. Is it any wonder that an earlier prototype of FirstDate places such a big emphasis on free first meals? What else is there to do?If this sounds like a radical solution to you, it’s only because you haven’t been paying attention, because it’s already happening.It offers a fascinating window into what government-funded culture activities that are also not-so-secretly trying to get people to make babies could look like. Festival attendees were literally handed out bracelets to signal to other attendees their openness to a relationship, and yet, the reception from everyone I spoke to was almost unanimously positive (towards the event, not the bracelets).In a time of shuttering nightclubs, bookstores, theatre groups, and whatever else you’d consider a common social space, I’d argue that this kind of support is badly needed. And, I would wager that MSF’s bet on third spaces is more likely to produce happy couples (and babies, if you care about that) than this.Let the cosplayers meet their kindred souls at the government-funded con. Let the book lovers meet at the talk at the indie bookstore. And let the nightlife enthusiasts meet at the sober (or not so sober) rave.And if you don’t get the love of your life out of it, well, at least you’ll have had a good time doing it.

item.title: Show HN: Giving Opus 5.5 a simulated paint canvas
item.author: alstonite
item.content:encoded: The painters are AI models. Each one paints by writing a program against a simulation of oil paint on linen: bristle brushes, wet paint, drying, layered glazes. No image model is involved.Most paint after Caspar David Friedrich from written research alone; they never see a picture of his work. Others were given a free subject.Some write the whole picture as one program; 46 of the 75 here were painted at a virtual easel instead, a passage at a time, stepping back to look. Each round tried a different setup: by round. Painters at work: the studio, live.

item.title: Arch-specific SIMD in Go
item.author: Junyang Shao and David Chase
item.content:encoded:
Since Go 1.26, we have supported an experimental SIMD API. Now in Go 1.27, we support two more architectures: and .The new APIs can be accessed by setting when building a program. They are defined in the package. is the lower-level infrastructure that builds on, essentially the intrinsics layer in other languages. For exotic operations that only exist on a specific architecture, users can access them by transitioning from to (via and ). For details, please refer to the simd blog post.For readers with prior knowledge of SIMD intrinsics in other languages, you might find that our API does not directly mirror the underlying hardware instructions:We give our APIs sensible names: e.g., instead of , we just call it .We leave some architecture details to compiler optimizations rather than exposing them in the API: e.g., instead of _mm512_maskz_add_ps(m, x, y), we optimize into the same instruction.These design decisions make our APIs smaller and more accessible, and they also happily make the implementation much easier.For readers without prior knowledge of SIMD intrinsics, we hope our low-level API is a natural and pleasant journey for you.Please share your feedback and comments. Anything about usability, performance, etc., is appreciated. The parent issue for this project is #73787.SIMD stands for Single Instruction, Multiple Data. SIMD instructions operate on wide registers (128-bit, 256-bit, or more) containing multiple 8- to 64-bit elements, performing operations across all elements in parallel. Wider registers and parallel execution provide a significant performance boost to algorithms that can take advantage of them.Until now, anyone who wanted to use SIMD in Go had to endure the friction of writing assembly language. The new package is here to change that.The goal is to support as many SIMD instructions across different architectures as possible. Currently, we have , , and available. Our support has the largest API surface, covering AVX, AVX2, and many AVX-512 extensions. Our support currently covers NEON, with SVE and some SVE2 already on the way. Our support is also mostly complete, thanks to its well-defined 128-bit SIMD abstraction.Some users might be interested in matrix extensions on certain architectures, such as AMX and SME. We haven’t fully settled on how to represent matrices effectively in Go, so they are not yet supported, but we might support them in the future.The architecture-specific SIMD API is imported from . uses distinct struct types, such as , , or , to signal the shape and element type of each vector, and defines operations as methods on those types. At this moment, supports only fixed-width vector extensions. Scalable vector extensions like SVE and RVV will have different struct types to represent vectors. Mask types also come with vector-like shapes, e.g., .Across different vector widths, element types, and architectures, we use the same method name whenever operations are semantically identical:Regardless of vector width or architecture, element-wise addition is simply ; the type of determines which instruction to emit. Instead of 18 different function names for addition, there is only one method name.When instructions on different architectures look similar at a glance but differ in edge-case behavior, we give them distinct names so differences don’t silently bite you. For example, 16-byte table lookup on () zeros the output byte when the index is negative () and wraps modulo 16 otherwise, so we call it . On NEON () and (), any out-of-range index () zeros the output byte, so we call it .On , many 256-bit and 512-bit instructions operate independently within 128-bit lanes rather than across the entire register. We explicitly suffix those methods with (such as or ) to make the 128-bit lane boundary obvious.Methods require a receiver value, which doesn’t work for creating a vector from memory or a scalar. For those, provides package-level functions named with the target vector type:: In Go 1.27, loading and storing slices use the shortest names: archsimd.LoadFloat32x4(s []float32) Float32x4 and . For tail elements that may be shorter than a full vector, archsimd.LoadFloat32x4Part(s []float32) (Float32x4, int) zero-fills the remaining lanes and returns the number of elements loaded, paired with x.StorePart(s []float32) int.: Fixed-size array pointers use the suffix (archsimd.LoadFloat32x4Array(y *[4]float32) and x.StoreArray(y *[4]float32)), and archsimd.BroadcastFloat32x4(v float32) broadcasts a scalar to all lanes.Reinterpretations are type casts without any cost. SIMD algorithms frequently reinterpret bits across element types and widths.In the Go 1.26 experiment, we implemented this with methods, which suffered from a quadratic explosion of type pairs and couldn’t generalize to width-agnostic vectors in or SVE.In Go 1.27, we replace them with composable zero-cost conversions: reinterprets a signed integer or float vector as an unsigned integer vector of the same element width (e.g., Int32x4.ToBits() -> Uint32x4), and / converts back. on unsigned vectors changes the element width within the same register width. For example, if is an , then x.ReshapeToUint32s().BitsToFloat32() reinterprets the bits of as an at zero runtime cost.Different architectures encode vector masks very differently, e.g. mask registers on AVX-512, full vector bitmasks on AVX/AVX2, NEON, and , and predicate registers on SVE. To hide this hardware detail, provides opaque types (such as ) matching each vector shape:Comparisons like produce a . zeros elements where is false, and (which replaces from Go 1.26) selects elements from where is true and from where is false.The compiler peepholes mask operations with the surrounding instructions: on AVX-512, or compiles into a single zero-masked or merge-masked instruction; on AVX2, NEON, or , it lowers to the appropriate bitwise or blend/bitselect instruction.Portable algorithms like inner product can easily be implemented using the portable package, as shown in the companion simd blog post. However, we still expose to tap into exotic, architecture-specific instructions that do not fit into a portable intersection API, or instructions that can simply do things faster than what provides.On , the GFNI extension exposes GaloisFieldAffineTransform operations. Putting aside what a Galois Field is, these operations do a simple thing:// Each element of A is interpreted as a matrix of 8 rows of vectors of 8 bits. // Each element of x is interpreted as a vector of 8 bits. // The b argument is likewise a vector of 8 bits. // The result is z[i] = (A[i/8] * x[i]) + b. // // The matrix * and vector + follow the usual rules for linear algebra, // but based on AND and XOR for scalar * and + // // Asm: VGF2P8AFFINEQB, CPU Feature: AVX512GFNI func (x Uint8x16) GaloisFieldAffineTransform(A Uint64x2, b uint8) Uint8x16 Each 8x8 bit matrix is packed row-by-row into a single . Because any linear combination or permutation of the 8 bits within a byte can be written as an 8x8 bit matrix, this single instruction is a Swiss Army knife for byte-level bit manipulation.For example, reversing the bit order of every byte () normally requires nibble lookup tables, masks, shifts, and ORs in SIMD. With GaloisFieldAffineTransform, we can simply multiply each byte by the 8x8 anti-diagonal identity matrix () to reverse all 8 bits of 64 bytes at a time in a single instruction:/* Anti-diagonal 8x8 bit matrix (0x8040201008040201): [ 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 1 ] [ x7 ] [ x0 ] [ 0 0 0 0 0 0 1 0 ] [ x6 ] [ x1 ] [ 0 0 0 0 0 1 0 0 ] [ x5 ] [ x2 ] [ 0 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 ] * [ x4 ] = [ x3 ] [ 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 0 ] [ x3 ] [ x4 ] [ 0 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 ] [ x2 ] [ x5 ] [ 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] [ x1 ] [ x6 ] [ 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] [ x0 ] [ x7 ] */ func ReverseBits(dst, src []uint8) { if !archsimd.X86.AVX512GFNI() { // A slow fallback emulation impl, details omitted. slowReverseBits(dst, src) return } if len(src) > len(dst) { // Make sure src and dst are the same size src = src[:len(dst)] } revMatrix := archsimd.BroadcastUint64x8(0x8040201008040201) var v archsimd.Uint8x64 var i int for i = 0; i < len(src)-v.Len()+1; i += v.Len() { v = archsimd.LoadUint8x64(src[i : i+v.Len()]) v.GaloisFieldAffineTransform(revMatrix, 0).Store(dst[i : i+v.Len()]) } if i < len(src) { v, _ = archsimd.LoadUint8x64Part(src[i:]) v.GaloisFieldAffineTransform(revMatrix, 0).StorePart(dst[i:]) } } Another example is matrix transpose. On , the permutation instructions are shaped in a non-portable way, so using is cumbersome and might incur emulations. An efficient implementation can be written more directly in . The example below transposes an 8-by-8 matrix of 32-bit integers in registers on using AVX2’s 128-bit lane-grouped interleaves (, ) and cross-lane permutations (ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped, ):func Transpose8(a0, a1, a2, a3, a4, a5, a6, a7 archsimd.Int32x8) ( b0, b1, b2, b3, b4, b5, b6, b7 archsimd.Int32x8) { if !archsimd.X86.AVX2() { // A slow fallback emulation impl, details omitted. return slowTranspose8(a0, a1, a2, a3, a4, a5, a6, a7) } /* LOW HIGH a0: abcd efgh a1: ijkl mnop a2: qrst uvwx a3: 0123 4567 a4: ABCD EFGH a5: IJKL MNOP a6: QRST UVWX a7: 89yz YZ$@ */ t0 := a0.InterleaveLoGrouped(a1) // t0 = aibj emfn t1 := a0.InterleaveHiGrouped(a1) // t1 = ckdl gohp t2 := a2.InterleaveLoGrouped(a3) // t2 = q0r1 u4v5 t3 := a2.InterleaveHiGrouped(a3) // t3 = s2t3 w6x7 t4 := a4.InterleaveLoGrouped(a5) // t4 = AIBJ EMFN t5 := a4.InterleaveHiGrouped(a5) // t5 = CKDL GOHP t6 := a6.InterleaveLoGrouped(a7) // t6 = Q8R9 UYVZ t7 := a6.InterleaveHiGrouped(a7) // t7 = SyTz W$X@
a0 = t0.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t2) // a0 = aiq0 emu4 a1 = t0.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t2) // a1 = bjr1 fnv5 a2 = t1.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t3) // a2 = cks2 gow6 a3 = t1.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t3) // a3 = dlt3 hpx7 a4 = t4.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t6) // a4 = AIQ8 EMUY a5 = t4.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t6) // a5 = BJR9 FNVZ a6 = t5.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t7) // a6 = CKSy GOW$ a7 = t5.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t7) // a7 = DLTz HPX@
b0 = a0.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a4) // b0 = aiq0 AIQ8 b1 = a1.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a5) // b1 = bjr1 BJR9 b2 = a2.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a6) // b2 = cks2 CKSy b3 = a3.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a7) // b3 = dlt3 DLTz b4 = a0.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a4) // b4 = emu4 EMUY b5 = a1.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a5) // b5 = fnv5 FNVZ b6 = a2.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a6) // b6 = gow6 GOW$ b7 = a3.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a7) // b7 = hpx7 HPX@
return } When walking through the examples above, you might have a few questions:What is archsimd.X86.AVX512GFNI(), and can I omit it?Why is the strided loop written as i = 0; i < len(src)-v.Len()+1; i += v.Len(), instead of i = 0; i + v.Len() <= len(src); i += v.Len()?Why does take 8 vector parameters rather than a struct or an array?At first glance these choices might look like minor stylistic preferences, but each of them is chosen for an important performance or correctness reason:CPU feature checks (, )On , we provide runtime feature checks like , , , and extension checks like or ; on , NEON is always available, and we provide checks for optional extensions like , , and . The compiler doesn’t know ahead of time whether the machine running your binary supports optional SIMD extensions. If you don’t guard your SIMD code with the appropriate feature check, your program may crash with on hardware that lacks the instruction.Just as importantly, CPU feature checks act as compiler optimization hints. For example, AVX-512 supports hardware merge-masking on instruction outputs. How the compiler lowers on a 128-bit or 256-bit vector depends on which CPU features are known to be available. If the code is not guarded by , the compiler must conservatively emit a vector followed by a instruction. Inside an block, however, the compiler knows AVX-512 is available and fuses the sequence into a single merge-masked AVX-512 instruction.Bounds check elimination in strided loopsHow you write the loop bound determines whether the compiler’s pass can eliminate slice bounds checks inside the loop. In , the addition could theoretically overflow to a negative if were near , which prevents the compiler from proving that is always non-negative and in-bounds. Writing avoids that potential overflow, allowing the loop body to compile with zero bounds checks.Keeping vectors in registers (avoiding large composite types) passes 8 vector parameters rather than a struct of 8 fields or an array because Go’s ABI and SSA backend currently place large composite types in memory rather than in registers (a known issue tracked at #24416). Because SIMD vectors are 16 to 64 bytes each, spilling them to the stack hurts performance much more than spilling scalar values. This applies to both function parameters and local variables, so avoid wrapping SIMD vectors inside large arrays or structs in hot loops. There are ongoing efforts to promote composite memory accesses back into registers, which have not yet landed in Go 1.27.In Go 1.27, supports (AVX, AVX2, and AVX-512), (NEON), and (WebAssembly 128-bit SIMD) out of the box. Whether you are on an Intel/AMD machine, an server or Apple Silicon Mac (M1/M2/M3/M4), or targeting WebAssembly, you can try natively right away:GOEXPERIMENT=simd go test simd/archsimd/... You can also cross-test (or via Rosetta emulation on Apple Silicon) by setting :# Run wasm SIMD tests using a WASI runtime: GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm GOEXPERIMENT=simd go test simd/archsimd/...
# Or run amd64 AVX2 tests on Apple Silicon via Rosetta: GOARCH=amd64 GOEXPERIMENT=simd go test simd/archsimd/... We’re interested in all sorts of feedback! Early users have already helped us catch bugs (such as #77582) and identify places where code generation or API ergonomics could be improved. We tried hard to pick clear, consistent names and cover the most useful instructions, but is a massive API surface and there is always room to improve.For Go 1.28 and beyond, we are actively working on completing SVE and SVE2 support in (introducing width-agnostic scalable vector types like backed directly by hardware SVE registers and predicates) and wiring it into . We also plan to expand to additional architectures such as , , , and , improve register promotion for composite types, and continue filling in instructions and compiler optimizations based on community feedback.
